But may the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little while, perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you. To him be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.

echoes.text: Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.
echoes.note: 'God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble' is a near-verbatim citation of Proverbs 3:34 LXX (which reads 'God' for MT 'he'/'the Lord'), introduced with proverbial authority; the same LXX form is quoted at James 4:6.
echoes.lxxText: The Lord resists the proud; but he gives grace to the humble.

echoes.text: When they cast down, you shall say, ‘be lifted up.’ He will save the humble person.
echoes.note: 'When they are cast down... the humble person he saves' (LXX: God 'will save the one of lowly eyes') feeds the humility-then-exaltation logic of 'humble yourselves... that he may exalt you.'

echoes.text: I know that the king of Egypt won’t give you permission to go, no, not by a mighty hand. I will reach out my hand and strike Egypt with all my wonders which I will do in its midst, and after that he will let you go.
echoes.note: 'The mighty hand of God' is the fixed exodus idiom for God's powerful, delivering action (the 'mighty hand' that brought Israel out of Egypt); here it frames the suffering exiles' submission under and rescue by that same hand.

echoes.text: Or has God tried to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, by war, by a mighty hand, by an outstretched arm, and by great terrors, according to all that Yahweh your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?
echoes.note: The recurrent Deuteronomic formula of God acting 'by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm' establishes 'the mighty hand of God' as a deliverance idiom underlying 5:6.

echoes.text: and I will bring you out from the peoples, and will gather you out of the countries in which you are scattered, with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out;
echoes.note: 'I will bring you out... with a mighty hand' applies the exodus 'mighty hand' to a restoration-from-exile context, fitting 1 Peter's address to elect exiles under God's hand.

echoes.text: Cast your burden on Yahweh, and he will sustain you. He will never allow the righteous to be moved.
echoes.note: 'Casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you' closely renders 'Cast your burden on the Lord, and he will sustain you' (LXX Ps 54:23), the clearest scriptural source for the anxiety-casting exhortation.

echoes.text: Commit your way to Yahweh. Trust also in him, and he will do this:
echoes.note: 'Commit your way to the Lord; trust in him, and he will act' offers a parallel trust-and-cast-upon-God motif reinforcing Psalm 55:22 behind 5:7.

echoes.text: They open their mouths wide against me, lions tearing prey and roaring.
echoes.note: The enemies 'open wide their mouths at me, like a ravening and roaring lion' supplies the 'roaring lion seeking to devour' image for the devil; the suffering-righteous-one context of Psalm 22 fits the persecuted readers.

His sons went and held a feast in the […]
echoes.note: 'The satan' as the accusing adversary who roams the earth (Job 1:7; 2:2) and tests the righteous stands behind 'your adversary, the devil, walks around... seeking whom he may devour,' and behind the call to withstand him steadfast in faith.

echoes.text: As a roaring lion or a charging bear, so is a wicked ruler over helpless people.
echoes.note: 'Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people' contributes the roaring-lion image of a predatory oppressor, apt for the persecuting power the devil energizes.

echoes.text: lest they tear apart my soul like a lion, ripping it in pieces, while there is no one to deliver.
echoes.note: 'Lest like a lion they tear my soul apart' adds to the stock of lament psalms portraying the enemy as a devouring lion behind 5:8.

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”
echoes.note: Satan standing to accuse the high priest, and the Lord rebuking him, reinforces the adversary/accuser background to the devil whom believers are to resist.

echoes.text: Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. The king spoke and said to Daniel, Your God whom you serve continually, he will deliver you. Then the king went to his palace, and passed the night fasting; neither were instruments of music […]
echoes.note: Daniel's faithful endurance in the lions' den, delivered by God, is a possible typological resonance for steadfastly withstanding the roaring lion amid suffering.

pericopes.text: Through Silvanus, our faithful brother, as I consider him, I have written to you briefly, exhorting, and testifying that this is the true grace of God in which you stand. echoes.text: Flee out of the midst of Babylon, and save every man his life; don’t be cut off in her iniquity: for it is the time of Yahweh’s vengeance; he will render to her a recompense. Babylon has been a golden cup in Yahweh’s hand, who made all the earth drunken: the nations have drunk of her wine; therefore the nations are mad. Babylon is suddenly fallen and destroyed: wail for her; take balm for her pain, if so be she may be healed.
echoes.note: 'She who is in Babylon' uses Babylon as a cryptonym for Rome, the imperial power; Jeremiah's oracles against Babylon as the place of exile and judgment supply the typology by which the church in Rome is figured as God's people in 'Babylon.'

echoes.note: Daniel's depiction of faithful exiles living under Babylon's empire establishes 'Babylon' as the type of the dominating pagan power among whom the elect sojourn, supporting the Babylon=Rome cryptonym.

echoes.note: 'By the rivers of Babylon... we wept' crystallizes Babylon as the archetypal land of exile, resonating with 1 Peter's framing of its readers as elect exiles greeted from 'Babylon.'

The noise of a multitude is in the mountains, as of a great people; the noise of an uproar of the kingdoms of the nations gathered together! Yahweh of Armies […]
echoes.note: Isaiah's burden against Babylon contributes to the prophetic Babylon-as-doomed-imperial-power tradition that makes Babylon an apt cryptonym for Rome.
